Before diving into the technical details of the calculations, it is useful to situate financial mathematics in its historical context: it is the culmination of several centuries of reflection on credit, money, and the measurement of economic time.

## The ancient origins of interest-bearing loans

Interest-bearing loans have been attested since antiquity: Mesopotamian tablets dating from around 2000 BCE already mention interest rates on loans of grain or silver. The practice, however, was long the object of moral and religious condemnation — usury (excessive interest, or even any interest at all according to certain doctrines) was denounced by numerous religious traditions, which slowed the development of sophisticated financial techniques for much of the Middle Ages in Europe.

## Fibonacci and the spread of commercial calculation

In the 13th century, the Italian mathematician Leonardo Fibonacci published the *Liber Abaci* (1202), which spread Arabic numerals and commercial calculation methods directly useful to merchants throughout Europe: currency conversion, profit calculation, and the first elements of interest calculation. This work marks an important step in the mathematical formalization of commercial and financial operations.

## The formalization of compound interest

The clear distinction between simple and compound interest, as well as the first tables of present and future values, truly developed from the 17th century on, carried by the growth of international trade, chartered companies, and the first forms of insurance and life annuities. The mathematicians of the era (including some close to the nascent field of probability, such as in the work related to life annuities) laid the foundations of modern actuarial calculation.

## The rise of bond and stock markets

Organized bond markets developed from the 17th–18th century in Europe, notably to finance state spending (wars, infrastructure). The Amsterdam Stock Exchange, considered one of the first modern stock exchanges, enabled organized trading of financial securities from the 17th century onward. Stock markets, for their part, developed with the rise of large joint-stock companies (the Dutch East India Company) and then more broadly with 19th-century industrialization.

## Modern portfolio theory and asset pricing

The 20th century saw the emergence of a genuine mathematical theory of finance: Harry Markowitz formalized modern portfolio theory in 1952 (the return–risk relationship, diversification), for which he received the Nobel Prize in Economics in 1990. In 1973, Fischer Black, Myron Scholes, and Robert Merton published the option pricing model that bears their names, the foundation of modern financial engineering. These advances, although going beyond the scope of this introductory course, all rest on the basic building blocks studied here: discounting, expected return, and risk measurement.

## Summary timeline

| Period | Landmark event |
| --- | --- |
| c. 2000 BCE | First written traces of interest-bearing loans (Mesopotamia) |
| 1202 | Publication of Fibonacci's *Liber Abaci*, spread of commercial calculation in Europe |
| 17th century | Rise of the Amsterdam Stock Exchange, first actuarial calculations on life annuities |
| 17th–19th century | Development of government bond markets and stock markets |
| 1952 | Harry Markowitz's modern portfolio theory |
| 1973 | Black–Scholes–Merton option pricing model |
| 2000s to today | Generalization of numerical and algorithmic tools in financial management |
